passages.happening: In the seventeenth year of Pekah, Ahaz son of Jotham becomes king of Judah at twenty and reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem. ‘And unlike David his father, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God’ (verse 2). He walks in the ways of the kings of Israel ‘and even sacrificed his son in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites’ (verse 3). He sacrifices and burns incense at the high places, on the hills and under every green tree (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Ahaz reigned in the 730s and 720s BC; common reckonings give about 735 to 715 BC, though the links with Hezekiah's dates are contested. Until now Judah's kings have mostly been graded as doing right, with the high places left standing. Ahaz is the first king of Judah in about a century to be judged without any qualification, and his sins match the worst of the north.

The chapter is a hinge in the book. It prepares for the fall of Samaria in chapter 17 and for the contrast of chapters 18 to 20, where Ahaz's son Hezekiah faces the same empire and trusts the LORD instead.

The law forbade sacrificing a child in the fire, and it linked the practice with the peoples the LORD had driven out.
passages.later: The law said, ‘Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire’ (Deuteronomy 18:10). Through Jeremiah the LORD said of such sacrifices, ‘something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind’ (Jeremiah 7:31).
passages.hard:
Did Ahaz really sacrifice his son, and how could a king of David's line do such a thing?

The Hebrew says that Ahaz made his son pass through the fire. Some interpreters have argued that this means a dedication ritual in which a child passed near or through flames without being killed. Most scholars read it as child sacrifice, because Chronicles speaks of him burning his sons, because Deuteronomy describes the nations burning their children to their gods, and because the prophets call the practice the shedding of innocent blood. The BSB follows that majority reading. The text names the act as an abomination and does not describe it, and these notes do the same.

How a king of David's line could do it is the chapter's point. In moments of desperate threat, ancient kings sometimes offered their children for a god's help, as the king of Moab did in chapter 3. Ahaz, facing two armies, turned to the gods of the nations and the power of Assyria instead of the LORD. The narrator does not soften it. The line through which God had promised his kingdom was capable of the worst sins of the peoples around it, and the promise survived because of God's faithfulness, not the kings'.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The worst sin of the nations reached the house of David. Ask what pressures can lead people to sacrifice their own children's good for their own security. And ask what it means that God kept his promise to David through kings who did not deserve it.

passages.happening:
Rezin king of Aram and Pekah king of Israel march on Jerusalem and besiege Ahaz, but they cannot overcome him (verse 5). Rezin takes Elath back from Judah (verse 6).

Ahaz sends messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria: “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hands of the kings of Aram and Israel, who are rising up against me” (verse 7). He takes the silver and gold from the house of the LORD and the palace treasuries and sends it to the king of Assyria (verse 8). The Assyrian marches on Damascus, captures it, carries its people to Kir and puts Rezin to death (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The attack is often called the Syro-Ephraimite war, Ephraim being another name for the northern kingdom, about 734 to 732 BC. Rezin and Pekah seem to have wanted Judah in a coalition against Assyria, and when Ahaz refused they tried to put a king of their own choosing in his place.

Ahaz's words are the language of vassal treaties. A weaker king pledged service to a great king, who offered protection in return. In Judah's own tradition, the king of David's line was called God's son. By calling himself Tiglath-pileser's son, Ahaz hands that loyalty to Assyria. The word for his payment, shochad, normally means a bribe, the gift the law forbade judges to take. The narrator calls it purchase, paid with what belonged to the LORD's house.

Assyria came at once. Tiglath-pileser took Damascus in 732 BC, executed Rezin and deported the Arameans, ending the kingdom that had troubled Israel since Ahab. An Assyrian inscription lists Jehoahaz of Judah, the fuller form of Ahaz's name, among the kings who paid tribute. Kir was the Arameans' ancestral homeland, and Amos had foretold this very exile.
passages.later: In this crisis Isaiah met Ahaz with the LORD's word: ‘If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all’ (Isaiah 7:9). When Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, Isaiah announced one: ‘Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel’ (Isaiah 7:14). The Hebrew word can mean a young woman or a virgin, and readers debate it. The sign had meaning in Ahaz's own day, and Matthew sees its fullest meaning in the birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:23).
passages.asks: Ahaz faced a real threat and chose a rescue he could see over a promise he could not. Ask where you are tempted to buy security at the cost of faithfulness. And ask whose servant and son you have called yourself to be kept safe.

passages.happening:
Ahaz goes to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser. He sees an altar there and sends Uriah the priest a model and complete plans for it (verse 10). Uriah builds it before the king returns (verse 11). Ahaz comes back and offers his burnt offering, grain offering, drink offering and peace offerings on it (verses 12-13).

He moves the LORD's bronze altar from its place before the temple to the north side of the new one (verse 14), and commands that all the regular offerings be made on the great altar. ‘But I will use the bronze altar to seek guidance’ (verse 15), he says. Uriah does as he is told (verse 16). Ahaz cuts the frames off the bronze stands, takes down the bronze Sea from the bronze oxen and sets it on a stone base (verse 17). ‘And on account of the king of Assyria’ (verse 18) he removes the Sabbath canopy and closes the royal entryway. Ahaz dies, and his son Hezekiah reigns (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Whether the Damascus altar was Assyrian or Aramean in style is debated, and so is whether Assyria required its vassals to adopt its worship. Many scholars now think it generally did not, which would make Ahaz's changes his own choice to impress his overlord. The great altar became the center of the morning and evening offerings, and the bronze altar made in Solomon's time was set aside for the king's private inquiries. The stands, the basins and the Sea were probably stripped for their metal to pay tribute.

The word for the plans, tavnit, pattern, is the word used when God showed Moses the pattern of the tabernacle and when David gave Solomon the plan of the temple. Here the pattern comes from Damascus, and the priest builds by the king's instructions rather than God's. The word for model, demut, likeness, is the word for humanity made in God's likeness in Genesis.

The narrator lingers over each change in almost inventory-like detail so that the reader sees the temple redesigned around a foreign king. The phrase on account of the king of Assyria ties the chapter together. The temple still stands and the sacrifices go on, but the center of gravity has moved.
passages.later: God had told Moses, ‘You must make the tabernacle and design all its furnishings according to the pattern I show you’ (Exodus 25:9).
passages.asks: The temple kept its sacrifices while its true loyalty moved to Assyria. Ask how worship can continue on the outside while the heart's loyalty shifts elsewhere. And ask whose approval is shaping the way you worship, and how you would know.
